introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the complex equitable rights between mortgagors and mortgagees. It dissects the sacred Right of Redemption, the mortgagee's Right of Foreclosure, and the doctrines of Subrogation and Marshalling.

core_concepts.title: Right of Redemption (Section 60)
core_concepts.description:
The most fundamental right of a mortgagor.
- Rule: Once the principal money becomes due, the mortgagor has the absolute right to pay the money and require the mortgagee to return the property/documents.
- Maxim: 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. 
- Clog on Redemption: Any condition inserted in the mortgage deed that attempts to restrict, delay, or prevent the mortgagor from redeeming the property is a 'clog' and is completely **Void**. (e.g., 'If loan is not paid in 5 years, the right to redeem is lost forever' - Void condition).

core_concepts.title: Right of Foreclosure or Sale (Section 67)
core_concepts.description:
The counterpart right of the Mortgagee (Lender).
- Foreclosure: A court order absolutely debarring the mortgagor from their right to redeem the property. 
- Restriction: The remedy of foreclosure is ONLY available in a **Mortgage by Conditional Sale** or an **Anomalous Mortgage**. 
- Sale: In a Simple Mortgage or English Mortgage, the remedy is to sell the property via court order, not foreclosure. (Usufructuary mortgages generally have neither right; the lender just keeps enjoying the property until the debt clears itself).

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Subrogation (Section 92)
core_concepts.description:
Subrogation means 'substitution'.
- Rule: Any person (other than the mortgagor) who pays off a mortgage debt steps into the shoes of the mortgagee (lender) whose debt they paid off. They acquire all the rights that the original mortgagee had against the mortgagor.
- Example: A mortgaged a house to Bank B. C (a co-owner or subsequent buyer) pays off Bank B's loan. C is now 'subrogated' to the position of Bank B, and can enforce the mortgage against A.

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Marshalling (Section 81)
core_concepts.description:
Designed to protect junior creditors.
- Scenario: A mortgages two properties (X and Y) to Bank 1. Later, A mortgages ONLY property Y to Bank 2.
- Rule: If A defaults, Bank 2 can force Bank 1 to satisfy its debt out of property X first. Bank 1 should only touch property Y if property X isn't enough to cover Bank 1's loan. This ensures both lenders get paid without prejudicing Bank 1.

important_entities.name: Rights of Lessee (Section 108)
important_entities.significance: Under Sec 108(e), if the leased property is wholly destroyed or rendered substantially and permanently unfit for the purposes for which it was let (by fire, flood, mob violence), the lease becomes **voidable at the option of the lessee**. They can choose to terminate it and stop paying rent.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams often ask: 'Can a lender file a suit for foreclosure in a Simple Mortgage?' **NO**. The right of foreclosure is strictly limited to Mortgage by Conditional Sale and Anomalous mortgages. In a Simple Mortgage, the ONLY remedy is a suit for **Sale**.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Once a mortgage, always a mortgage
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: This means a mortgage cannot suddenly convert into an absolute sale just because of a harsh condition in the contract.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC Law Optional question asks about the clash between Section 60 (Redemption) and harsh lender contracts, invoke the doctrine against **Clog on Equity of Redemption** and declare such conditions void.
